name: John Kennedy

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: Veterans Day (Executive Session)
statements.title: Veterans Day (Executive Session)
sentences: Our Democratic colleagues may agree to some defense spending in a new budget, but they will extract, in return, much more domestic spending.
That we have a 6 percent budget deficit every year and $40 trillion in debt is not going to deter them.
Whether you agree with Iran or not, no one--no fairminded person, wants to have an Afghanistan.
I would take up that bill, and I would pass it and use the savings from abolishing or at least undermining that fraud and use it to pay down our debt.
If we don't confirm these people, my Democratic friends will not, I can assure you.
And my colleagues and I are committed to spending whatever time it takes between now and the end of the year, including Christmas Day, including Christmas Eve, and including Thanksgiving.
So if we are going to get money to our military, we need to do it now.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: LEGISLATIVE SESSION
statements.title: LEGISLATIVE SESSION
sentences: But if you look at this bill from 35,000 feet, what it really does is exempt colleges and universities and the NCAA from the antitrust laws.
We are all subject to the antitrust laws.
It violates the antitrust laws.
This bill exempts the colleges and universities and the athletic programs from the antitrust laws.
You may like what the bill does or you may dislike it, but what it does is give the NCAA and college sports teams and the universities an exemption from the antitrust laws.
But the point I am trying to make is, if we give the NCAA and we give the colleges and universities an exemption from the antitrust laws, it is going to cap the amount that these athletes can make.
So the fans are paying their fair share, but as best as I can tell, this bill doesn't do a damned thing for the fans.

If I am given the chance--and it doesn't look like I am going to be able to--I am going to offer an amendment that says, in return for the antitrust exemption and capping the amount of money that colleges and universities and coaches have to pay their athletes, you can't raise ticket prices on the fans more than 4 percent a year.
We are going to look back 5 years from now and realize that what President Trump has done in Iran and what Israel has done in Iran has made the world immeasurably safer.
But what the President has done and Israel has done--and they had the courage to do it--has made the world safer--not just the Middle East, the entire world.
Israel and America have gutted Iran like a fish.
It is not being reported by the press, but Iran today is immeasurably weaker.
Iran today--both the public and the private sector--is a sucking chest wound.
There are whole parts of Iran that look like something out of ``Mad Max'' 4.
I hate to see us have to do it to the Iranian people, but they have got 70 percent inflation.
We just increased sanctions even more so that planes can't fly in and out of Iran.
Iran has no air defenses anymore.
That means that we can send our bombers and fly anywhere we want to in our planes in Iran without worrying about being shot at--anywhere.
Right now, Iran doesn't have a nuclear weapons program.

Our intelligence and Israeli intelligence will know within 5 minutes if Iran restarts its nuclear weapons program, and as soon as they do, because we have crushed them like a bug, we will know--and they have no air defenses-- and we can go in and bomb their program all over again.
I am not talking about the good people of Iran; I am talking about the leadership.
I know a lot of my colleagues--they have the right to their opinion-- have accused the President of everything except abandoning his children to wolves in terms of Iran.

President Trump has made the world immeasurably safer--not just the Middle East--immeasurably safer because he is the first President in our lifetime, along with Israel, to say: Iran, we have had enough of your BS.
I am not going to go into a lot of detail about the rules.
I will tell you who else wins, not that they need Congress' help: our college coaches.
Maybe, in the long run, if it makes college sports healthy, it will be in the best interests of the athletes so I am not going to weigh in on that.
Let's do something for the fans, but I don't know if I am going to get that opportunity.
I may offer it in a separate bill, but they probably won't let me bring it up, and I am going to just mention that.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT OF 2026--Motion to Proceed
statements.title: PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT OF 2026--Motion to Proceed
sentences: Mr. President, it is hard to know precisely what to believe about artificial intelligence.
I don't think that the American people--even though the polls show otherwise--really hate data centers.
I don't think that they really hate data centers.

I know that if you poll right now--this is true in Louisiana, but I think it is true nationwide--and ask folks: Do you support data centers, they will say the short answer is no; the long answer is hell no.
But I really don't think it is the data centers.

I also think the pushback is a result--I don't mean to get off on a tangent--but the pushback, it is the result of the fact that the AI CEOs, in selling the data centers, seem to have hired the former marketing director at Cracker Barrel or Bud Light because they have done a pretty lousy job of selling the product.

We had a chance to take a brandnew technology--cryptocurrency-- yesterday and make it part of the American financial system and give it a reasonable market structure and make it better and more for everybody, and we couldn't even do that.
What I am suggesting to you is that there are risks to artificial intelligence.
And by AI, I mean the advanced AI models that you can direct through agents to do all sorts of stuff.

So in my mind, if there is even a 1-percent chance that one of these AI models can shed its nature as a tool and become an independent species and start doing whatever the hell it wants to do, if there is even a 1-percent chance, we ought to take it seriously.
Well, I have got a bill, and it basically says that if you are going to sell an advanced AI model in the United States of America, it has got to have a kill switch.
It doesn't put the Federal Government or any government in charge of the kill switch.
It puts the companies who own the model in charge of the kill switch.
My bill would rely on them doing the right thing in exercising their own self-interests and using that kill switch when they need it.
Some of them have a kill switch but others don't.
A kill switch is basically an emergency shutoff.
My bill doesn't come up with a kill switch.
It doesn't tell the companies what kind of kill switch to do.

My bill would give the Department of Homeland Security 90 days to develop rules giving the private companies options for which kill switches they would use, but it would require them to have a kill switch.
All I want to do is say, if you are going to sell one of these AI models that could take on a life of its own, then you have to have a kill switch to reassert human control.

Therefore, notwithstanding rule XXII, I ask unanimous consent that the Senate proceed to the immediate consideration of S. 5417--that is my bill--which is at the desk; further, I ask that the bill be considered read a third time and passed and that the motion to reconsider be considered made and laid upon the table.
I think we are going to--and I am not being critical because I voted for it.
I think we are going to pass the bill to make the football coaches happy, but after that, I am not sure if we will get anything else done.
They suggested that in talking to themselves, if you looked--read the report: We know what we are doing is probably wrong, but we are going to do it anyway.
And this particular company--I am not going to mention the name because they are not the only ones, and I appreciate their coming forward and telling us.
My guess is, there is way less than a 1-percent chance that I am going to have a fire, but we have decided, through our representatives, we are not going to take that 1-percent chance.
We are not going to get up off of our ice-cold, lazy butts and address this anytime soon.
All of us probably ought to hide our heads in a bag, but we are not going to do that.
So we are not going to be able to have a rational debate and reach a decision about what and how we should, if in any way, regulate AI.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: AGOA EXTENSION ACT--Motion to Proceed--Continued
statements.title: AGOA EXTENSION ACT--Motion to Proceed--Continued
sentences: Ukraine has Putin down and is choking him.
We need to help Ukraine choke him to death.
I am doubly sorry the people of Ukraine are, but it is not going to stop until Putin understands--and we make him understand--that the costs of his barbarism outweigh the benefits.
For the first time since 2022, through sheer will and some big brains and help from Europe and help from the United States, Ukraine has Putin on the back foot.
I remember when Putin invaded in 2022.
All the experts said Putin is going to roll through Ukraine like thunder on a summer night; headed toward Kyiv, he is going to take it over.
We should have known then that the Ukrainian people are tough as a pine knot.
And I guarantee you, in his heart of hearts, Vladimir Putin wishes he never started that fight.
Putin thought time was on his side.
Ukraine is now the drone master of the universe.
Ukraine is producing more drones.
Ukraine is using those drones to overwhelm the Russian air defense.
Ukraine has figured out a way to overwhelm Russian air defenses so that some of those drones get through.
No part of Russia is safe right now because of these drones by Ukraine.
In late June, Ukrainian drones took out two oil refineries in a city called Ufa--I am probably mispronouncing it.
It means they don't have any diesel fuel.
Ukraine used drones to take out two of them--about $2 billion.
Recent polls--it is hard to get good data out of Russia because Putin has turned Russia into China.
Because between 30 and 40 percent of Russia's budget and Putin's budget--they are one and the same right now--comes from oil and gas.
But they finally faced reality, and they have stepped up and financially supported Ukraine.
And the American people generously supported Ukraine for a long time, and we still are sharing intelligence with them.
But this will cut off Putin's cash fund--one simple bill.
Election Integrity Madam President, No. 2, let me talk about election integrity.
Let me tell you what I think of when I think of the SAVE Act.
So when I think of the SAVE Act, I am thinking of election integrity.
And, really, what the SAVE Act means to me is two things: It means you have to prove you are who you say you are in order to vote and in order to register to vote.
Rule No. 1, you have to prove you are who you say you are in order to register to vote and to vote.
The President does not want voting by mail.
If the people of Alaska or the people of New York or the people of Florida want to vote by mail, that is up to them and their State legislatures.
I think we need to take up that money bill, and I think part of it needs to be election integrity.
The States are going to need resources, and that is the whole purpose of the so-called SAVE Act in the budget resolution.

Now, it may be that we can put in a provision--I don't know; some big brains tell me it will work--that if we provide money to the States to implement election integrity, that if enough States participate, that it will become not just custom but law that these two rules apply.

I don't know if that is possible under the Budget Control Act, but I do know that the SAVE Act, right now--in addition to the two rules of election integrity that I talk about--involves money, and that is what we are going to try to do.
It is also true of the Russia sanctions bill, but it is especially true with respect to election integrity.

I can't tell you how many meetings I have been in, in the last 6 months, that should have been an email, that could have been an email, to talk about the Russia sanctions bill and to talk about election integrity and to try to get a consensus.

In no particular order, we need to pass the Russia sanctions bill; we need to pass the budget resolution, which will include election integrity; we need to confirm Todd Blanche; we need to pass the continuing resolution to keep government open until December 11; and we need to vote on the cryptocurrency bill, which we have spent years on.
And I will never forget what President Zelenskyy said.
And if there is a motion made on this floor to have us remain here until we get our work done, I am going to vote yes.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: Iran (Executive Session)
statements.title: Iran (Executive Session)
sentences: Mr. President, last night, I read the memorandum of understanding between the United States and Iran.

And for 60 days, Iran has removed its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, which means ships containing oil and natural gas and fertilizer can go back and forth just like they were before the conflict started.
The other practical consequence is that Iran will be able to start selling its oil again for 60 days.

Now, in the document, Iran says that it is willing to negotiate for 60 days to get rid of its fissile material that it can use to make a nuclear weapon, including, but not limited to, its centrifuges that it uses to enrich the uranium.
And in the document, Iran says: We are willing to renounce our desire to have a nuclear weapon.
And in the document, Iran says: For 60 days, we are willing to negotiate some sort of inspection protocol so that the world can go in and make sure that Iran is telling the truth.
Now, this might be a good time to say that--as I have said all week and as I have said in another context before--I trust the Iranian Government like I trust gas station sushi.
The Iranian Government--not the Iranian people--the Iranian Government are a bunch of religious nuts.
My experience with the Iranian Government--not the Iranian people--is that they lie like they breathe.

The other thing that I am certain of today is that Iran is immeasurably weaker than it was a year ago, than it was before the United States and Israel bombed their nuclear facilities last June, and before the conflict that we have watched transpire over the last couple of months--immeasurably weaker.
There are whole swathes of Iran that look like the aftermath of a bar brawl.
There are entire regions in Iran that look like something out of ``Mad Max'' 4.
The private sector--Iran has got--I don't know how anybody is eating or living in Iran.
In Iran today--and I regret this, but it had to be done.
In Iran today, its public and private sectors are held together with spit and duct tape, and all the President has done is said: OK.
For 60 days, I am going to give peace a chance and give you a chance to do what you say you are going to do.
We will know soon, and I hope it works.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: Appropriations (Executive Session)
statements.title: Appropriations (Executive Session)
sentences: President Xi in China, President Putin in Russia, and the Ayatollah in Iran have formed a partnership.

And their goal--President Xi and his two junior partners--is to have Russia dominate Eastern Europe, to have Iran dominate the Middle East, to have China dominate the Indo-Pacific, and have the freedom to roam throughout Sub-Saharan Africa and South America and the Arctic and space.
I do not want America to be the world's policeman, but I don't want Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin and the Ayatollah in Iran to be either.

Now, there are only three ways to do that, as you know, Mr. President: Through our budget, the regular appropriation process; through what is called a supplemental bill, which deals just with defense spending; and through the process of reconciliation.
President Trump has proposed a 42-percent increase in defense spending.
I think, if everybody were pulling in the same direction, we could probably do a 20- to 25-percent increase in defense spending in our regular budget.
I will give you one example, at least from my perspective.
Passing a supplemental bill is not going to work for reasons--the same reasons that we are not going to be able to pass a budget, about which I will talk in a second.
And if I am wrong, I will come to this floor and I will say: I was wrong; I apologize.
Now, they know we are not going to agree to that.

And I think that if we went to our Democratic colleagues today and said, ``OK, you win; we are going to spend 25 percent more on defense, and we will spend 25 percent more on nondefense; let's vote,'' every single Democrat would vote no.
If I am wrong, I will apologize.

We are going to get to September, and Republicans are going to say: Well, we don't have a budget because you refused to talk about it, because you want chaos, because Senator Schumer told you to create chaos, because the Graham Platner wing of the Democratic Party told Senator Schumer to tell you to create chaos.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: Department of Homeland Security (Executive Calendar)
statements.title: Department of Homeland Security (Executive Calendar)
sentences: But a very important part is not: the Border Patrol and ICE.
At one point my Democratic friends agreed to fund Border Patrol and ICE.
Unless you are industrial-strength stupid, you know that illegal immigration is illegal.
And that is what our Border Patrol agents and ICE agents do--they enforce the law.
And it falls to the responsibility of the Department of Homeland Security, in part through Border Patrol and ICE, to find out.
Why do we now need Border Patrol and ICE more than ever?
It could be that the people that President Biden put in charge of immigration and securing the border were not qualified to play dead in a western movie.

I am talking the Platner wing of the Democratic Party, the Mayor Mamdani wing of the Democratic Party, the Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez wing of the Democratic Party, the wing of the Democratic Party that is in control-- some of them believe that vetting people at the border is racist.
It doesn't matter that every other country in the world vets people at their border.

These members of the--whatever you want to call it-- progressive wing, loon wing, woketopus wing--whatever you want to call that wing of the Democratic Party, they think that vetting people at the border is racist.
There are other folks who support open borders for political reasons.
And more even to that point, we have to have Border Patrol and ICE officers to do it.

And what we have seen at the Delaney Hall detention center: We have seen ICE officers and some Border Patrol officers; we have seen the protestors cursing at them and spitting at them and threatening their families and hitting them and scratching them and biting them and blocking ingress and egress in and out of the detention center.
I think the Border Patrol and ICE and the State law enforcement officials in New Jersey have shown a lot of restraint.
Most Border Patrol agents, most ICE agents, most cops, they will leave you alone unless you do illegal stuff.
We need to vote to fund Border Patrol and ICE.
I am sorry that my Democratic colleagues have taken the position that they want to defund ICE.
I am sorry that they have taken the position they want to defund the Border Patrol.
All we will be voting on: Do we or do we not want to fund Border Patrol and ICE?

And then they changed their minds, and they said: No, we are not going to do it, which forced Republicans, if we want to see that portion of DHS funded, to proceed under what we call reconciliation where we don't need Democratic votes.

Now, we have made it as complicated as hell, as the Federal Government is wont to do, but this is what the child and dependent care tax credit basically does: Basically, if you are a mom and dad and you are working and you have to pay for childcare--which is outrageously expensive; I am not blaming the childcare providers, but it is just really expensive--under the child and dependent care tax credit, we will pay a portion of your childcare expenses.
For about 4 million working families, they are going to get more money to pay for childcare.
For many families, that is going to mean an extra $900 a family to pay for their childcare.
We also have another program--way too complicated--called the employer-provided childcare credit, 45F.

So that is the second way that we have, at the Federal level, to try to help people pay for their childcare.

To make a long story short, which sometimes is difficult for me to do, basically, in the One Big Beautiful Bill, we have given employers all across America more money so they can, in turn, help their employees by giving them more money to pay for childcare.

I could talk about the paid family and medical leave credits.
It is not just the downpayment.
One way to increase the supply of housing is to change your zoning laws.

You know, we all need zoning laws.

You change zoning laws, whatever you do.
They changed their zoning laws.

I am not going to go into that, but I do want to highlight one of the things we did--one among, frankly, thousands in the One Big Beautiful Bill--to try to help people in the middle class who are scared and who are angry.
I will give you an example--and the Presiding Officer knows this.
Basically, if you have a child in America, we will give you a certain amount of money to defray the cost of raising that child.
We are doing a lot of stuff, but I will just mention one in particular: housing.
I have had it put on the crypto bill that we are going to mark up tomorrow.
We have passed it twice, and it is in front of the House now, but in case something goes wrong over there, I am going to send it to them again through the crypto bill.
It doesn't tell local government how to do their job; it just tells them: We will give you extra money if you will do your job.
We are not going to tell you how to do your business.
But if you will encourage more housing built by the private sector and increase housing starts, we will give you extra money from that pool of $3 billion from community development block grants.
No. Senator Warren's bill and my bill wouldn't cost anything because, yes, we will reward with extra money those counties and cities that increase housing starts.
We are going to take it from the cities and counties that don't increase housing starts.
Whatever the magic words the Parliamentarian is telling me to say, I want to say it, and we will be recessed until we are supposed to come back.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: CARBON DIOXIDE
statements.title: CARBON DIOXIDE
sentences: Mr. President, I rise for two reasons: First, I talked last night about carbon capture--carbon dioxide capture--injection wells in Louisiana.
Carbon dioxide, while a naturally occurring gas that God created-- when you breathe, what you blow out is carbon dioxide.
The world couldn't exist without carbon dioxide.
But carbon dioxide is also a gas that is heavier than air, and it rises.
And while there are many good things about CO2, as we call it, one of the bad things is that carbon dioxide acts as a blanket over our world.
And carbon dioxide acts as this blanket, and it holds in the Earth's heat.
And that can--that can affect your climate and your temperature.
That is what all this discussion about carbon dioxide is all about.
A number of years ago, Congress decided to encourage companies that produce carbon dioxide.
And one of the ways you also produce carbon dioxide, I should also add, is by burning fossil fuels.

So a petrochemical plant, which uses natural gas when it produces the chemicals, it also produces CO2, or carbon dioxide, just like I have been producing it as I have been breathing while we are talking.
In any event, Congress passed a statute and said: We want to try to minimize the production of carbon dioxide, which can affect our climate when we burn fossil fuels.
So Congress came up with this idea of paying companies money to capture that carbon dioxide so that it is not released into the atmosphere--and, boy, do we pay a bunch of money.
We are paying it to private companies to capture this carbon dioxide.
One of the things that companies do when they produce the carbon dioxide and they want to capture it--after they capture it, they have to do something with it.
I am not here to debate the merits of carbon capture and what we call carbon capture sequestration.
All I am saying is that under Louisiana law, if you own property and you don't want a company drilling a well and putting carbon dioxide under your property, you should have the right to say no.
I am not saying they were right or wrong to do it, just like I am not debating the merits--or lack thereof--of carbon capture and sequestration.

All I am saying is that under my State law, if a company captures this carbon dioxide and wants to drill a well and inject it beneath the surface and if they want to put it on my property and I don't want them to put it on my property, then they come to me and say ``I want to drill a well and inject carbon dioxide,'' I am entitled to say ``Yep, you got it.
Some States call it eminent domain.
All I am saying is, in the great State of Louisiana, we go about this business of debating carbon capture and climate change and that sort of thing.

If you own property, which, under my State constitution and the Federal Constitution, is an inalienable/unalienable right--you have the right to own property in America--and if a company wants to drill a well on your property and put carbon dioxide down there and you don't want them to, then you ought to have a right to say no, and the State can't make you, and the companies can't make you.

If the powers that be in my State start bullying people--I am not saying they will, but if they start bullying people and taking their property when they don't want to give it up, in order to inject carbon dioxide beneath their land without their permission or consent, then I am going to have something to say about it because this money that we are paying companies to do that is from a Federal statute.
It is called, I think, a 45Q tax credit.
That 45Q tax credit can be changed.
I am not going to regive that speech.

sentences: But I want to thank the members of law enforcement who prevented what could have been a very serious tragedy Saturday night.
I would do it again in a heartbeat.
In fact, if you look at the numbers today, we still protect the United Kingdom and NATO and our friends in Europe.
The American taxpayer still puts up 60 percent of total NATO defense spending today.
Now, when Iran fires a missile at their base in Cyprus, they can barely find a ship to send down there.
Sir Keir Starmer, the Prime Minister of the UK, published his plan for the military and military spending.
Carbon Dioxide Mr. President, I want to spend my last few minutes on another topic.
I want to talk about carbon dioxide.
We all know, we have all heard carbon dioxide--CO2--is a gas.
CO2 is composed of one atom of carbon and two atoms of oxygen, and it is produced naturally.
When we breathe out, for example, we breathe out carbon dioxide.
And even though carbon dioxide has all these extraordinarily beneficial uses, one of the downsides of it is that it is a fairly heavy gas.
But it does rise, and it is what is called a greenhouse gas.
That is why you hear some folks talk about global warming and climate change.
When it burns fossil fuels, natural gas usually, it produces CO2-- carbon dioxide.
Now, you would hope that companies--many of them became during the Biden years very woke, and they criticized anybody who asked questions about President Biden's climate change plan.
But the other reason they were so high on carbon capture is because the Federal Government was giving them bucketloads of money to capture this carbon.
It is called the 45Q tax credit.
We will actually pay these companies--like a petrochemical company--to capture carbon and inject it into the ground in the interest of our environment and climate.
So while I want to believe that the companies capture the carbon in the interest of the environment, they are being paid a whole bunch of money to do it as well.
So, anyway, we are paying companies a whole bunch of money to go capture this carbon and inject it in the ground.
I know in other cases there have been CO2 pipelines--carbon dioxide pipelines-- transmitting carbon dioxide that have ruptured and injured people.

Now, our constitution also goes on to say, because we are a practical people in Louisiana: This right to own property is subject to reasonable statutory restrictions and the reasonable exercise of the police power.
I think some States call it eminent domain.

But the people in Louisiana have just discovered that the companies that I talked about who are being paid this Federal money--$85 a ton to capture carbon and inject it into the ground--can also take people's land to put in an injection well.
I am not taking sides in terms of carbon capture.
But we have got a lot of people in my State that are very suspect about the wisdom of this carbon capture.

And if someone in my State who owns a piece of property--it is usually in my rural areas--who owns 50 acres that was handed down from their dad and mom and their dad and mom and their dad and mom, if a company wants to come in and pay them to put in an injection well and put carbon dioxide underneath their land and those land owners are OK with that, I am OK with it.

This is what it says: Any storage operator-- That is the guy or gal who wants to put carbon dioxide under the ground-- Any storage operator is hereby authorized, after obtaining any permit and any certificate of public convenience and necessity from the commissioner-- That means they get the permission of the State. . . . [can] exercise the power of eminent domain and expropriate [take] needed property.
I am going to keep reading, but I really regret that they have given in to their appetitive desires and lost some of their objectivity.
I support continuing to do that.
But just based on paying them $85 a ton, by 2030, we will be spending about $30 billion.
So we are going to take your property, but we are going to pay you full price.

sentences: Mr. President, I am going to give you a name: Tony Hanagan.

sentences: I want to talk, just for a few minutes, about digital assets.
Some people refer to them as crypto or cryptocurrency.
The Senate Banking Committee is in the process, as we should be, of considering market structure legislation for digital assets, for Bitcoin, for crypto.
I remember when blockchain technology started--many of us do.
Today, one in five Americans is on cryptocurrency.
Those who are in the cryptocurrency business and in the blockchain technology business don't know whom to talk to in the Federal Government.
The Securities and Exchange Commission has announced, under President Biden, that it has jurisdiction over digital assets, and so did the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the CFTC.
We passed the GENIUS Act, as the Presiding Officer knows.
It regulates stablecoins, which is only one part of the digital assets business.
But it is only a small portion of the digital assets market.
The House has passed a bill called the CLARITY Act, which does just what I have been talking about, providing some market structural legislation for the crypto industry, the digital assets industry.
But the Senate has decided not to take up the CLARITY Act.
But the thinking seems to be that the Senate needs to start over and draft our own digital assets market structure bill that complements the CLARITY Act, which is already passed by the House.

We have to be sure, in this legislation, given that one in five Americans owns cryptocurrency--we have to make sure, in this legislation, that we are striking the right balance in jurisdiction between the CFTC and the SEC.
The banking community, after we passed the GENIUS Act--remember the GENIUS Act was just about stablecoins.

The Banking Committee is arguing--rather, the banking community, our banks, are arguing, very persuasively, that there were some mistakes made in the GENIUS Act, which, as I just said, regulates stablecoins.
If we did make some mistakes in the GENIUS Act with respect to American banks, I want us to correct it.

But my point is that we are going to have to take up that issue as well in the hearing because the banking community would like us to amend the larger digital asset market structure legislation to accommodate their concerns about the mistakes, if any, that we made in the GENIUS Act.
It is a way, basically, to trade a stock using blockchain technology without owning stock.
Cryptocurrency is--well, it is currency in the eyes of many people.
And I can see the day when the American people will ask us to address the issues: Should deposit insurance cover cryptocurrency and digital assets?
I also think it would be appropriate in a hearing on this topic before we draft or vote on legislation to talk about the Clarity Act.
And I want to be able to compare the Clarity Act passed by the House with the Senate's market structure legislation.
But we also need to address the issue of what, if any, fiduciary responsibility those who participate in the digital assets markets have.
But when one in five Americans own cryptocurrency, it is certainly important.
So I will probably be talking about this issue several more times on the floor as the Senate moves forward with our digital assets market structure legislation.
I hope we will move it quickly, but I hope we will move deliberately.
I hope we will take the time to hold the hearings.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: GOVERNMENT FUNDING
statements.title: GOVERNMENT FUNDING
sentences: We didn't cut Medicaid in the One Big Beautiful Bill.
In fact, under our bill, Medicaid is going to increase 2 percent a year over the next 10 years.
What we did by reforming Medicaid, which Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez wants us to reverse, we cut out the waste and the fraud.
For example, we found out that there are--no kidding, I am not just making this up--we found out that there are 2.8 million people on Medicaid who are double-dipping in America.
They are either signing up for Medicaid in Louisiana and Mississippi double-dipping or signing up for Medicaid in Louisiana and they are signing up for the Affordable Care Act subsidies.
The second thing we did in our healthcare reforms in the One Big Beautiful Bill is to say you have to stop lying when you apply for Medicaid.
People could walk in, and the Medicaid folks would say: How much do you make a year?
We have found--for example, just in Louisiana, we did a statistical sample of the people on Medicaid in Louisiana.
Our auditors found 1,600 people on Medicaid who were making $100,000 a year or more.

We put a provision in our bill that the Congresswoman and the socialist wing of her party want us to take out that says: Look, if you are between the ages of 19 and 64 and you are able-bodied--we are not talking about a mother with a sick child in her arms--if you are able- bodied, if you are perfectly healthy, and if you don't have any dependent kids at home, then, if you qualify based on income, we will give you Medicaid.
That is what is called a work requirement.
Well, they are upset at us over the Affordable Care Act.
Let me tell you what all this is about with the Affordable Care Act.
Under ObamaCare, if you are a low-income American, you are entitled to Medicaid.
But if you are in the middle and if you make a little more money than the poverty level but you can't get insurance through your employer, we provide what is called the ObamaCare exchanges.
So when we talk about the ObamaCare subsidies, that is what we are talking about.
We are going to say that there are no income limits on ObamaCare--paid for by the taxpayer.
We have 24 million people on ObamaCare.
That added about 1.6 million people on ObamaCare.
ObamaCare was meant for people who make from roughly $30,000 a year to $130,000 a year for families of four.
Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez got very, very upset, as did the socialist wing of her party, when the President sent over what is called a rescission package.
We found $500,000 of American taxpayer money for electric buses in Rwanda.

There was $6 million for media organizations for the Palestinians; $833,000 for transgender people in Nepal; $300,000 for a pride parade in Lesotho; $882,000 for social media mentorship in Serbia; $4.2 million--we took it out, and the Congresswoman and the socialist wing of their party says we have to put that back in before they will open the government--$4.2 million for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and intersex people in the Western Balkans and Uganda.

Here is what the socialist wing of the Democratic Party, led by Congresswoman Ocasio- Cortez, has said to the American people and to the U.S. Congress and to the Republicans in Congress: If you, Republicans, don't agree to make the Federal Government $1.5 trillion--not million dollars, not billion dollars, $1.5 trillion--bigger, we are going to shut the government down.
I am not going to vote for that.
We are going to raise the limit.
Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez says: No. Until you agree to let them continue, to let anybody at any income level get subsidies, we are going to shut the government down.
I will just read you a few more that we took out that they are demanding we put back in.
All we are asking for is what we call a clean CR.
All we are asking for is just to further negotiate.
They know what we are asking for is reasonable.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: CLOTURE MOTION
statements.title: CLOTURE MOTION
sentences: That is what is happening in Ukraine.
And it is not fair to Ukraine.
This is a picture of people in Ukraine burying their dead.
Now, for 8 months, President Trump has tried to talk to President Putin in Russia--8 months.
And for 8 months, President Putin has made all kinds of promises--a lot of pretty words, a lot of play-acting--and he has done none of what he said he would do.
He has played--``he'' meaning President Putin.
President Putin says he wants peace, but he doesn't, and we know that now.
President Putin is not going to want peace until the costs of war are greater than peace.
For someone who has blood under his fingernails, for someone who has Stalin's taste for death-- and I am, of course, referring to Putin--it is simply a cost-benefit analysis.
We are going to have to do something if we all want peace--and we all say we do, including the people of Ukraine.

But in order to get peace and to get Putin to negotiate seriously, we are going to have to increase the costs and make the cost on him of prosecuting the war greater than the benefits of him being able to continue to do it.
Putin has completely transformed Russia.
Putin has turned Russia into a total authoritarian state.
Putin has converted Russia into a war economy.
It is very expensive, and Putin affords it by selling oil.
In fact, 40 percent of Putin's cash flow--the only way he has been able to prosecute this war is by selling oil.
Meantime, Putin is launching 800--not 80--800 drones and 800 missiles a night at the Ukrainian people, and he is not just aiming that weaponry at the Ukrainian soldiers.
The President met with Putin in Alaska, as we all know, and made a bunch of promises and completely reneged.
We are going to seize Russian assets if our legislation passes, and we are going to give those assets to Ukraine to prosecute the war.
You have probably heard that term, ``foreign reserves.'' They are used in trade to convert from one currency to another.
When the war--when Putin attacked Ukraine, Russia had $300-plus billion--some say it is as high as $320 billion--of assets in Europe and the United States; most of them are in Europe.
They originally were in debt securities, but we are talking cash now.
It has been sitting there, and it has been invested basically in money markets, and we have been sending the interest to Ukraine to help them fight the war.
It is a violation of international law for them to have invaded Ukraine and to be massacring these people.
We will give it in tranches, in smaller amounts as they need it, to Ukraine.
We will give it to Ukraine in tranches.
Ukraine can use that money to buy their own drones and to buy their own missiles.

Ukraine can use that money not to kill Russian civilians, but Ukraine can use that money to buy missiles to take out every single refinery in Russia, cut off their cash flow, take out every single oil refinery in Russia.

Ukraine can use that money to buy missiles to take out every single weapons production plant in Russia--every single one--and make President Putin understand that there is going to be a cost for him prosecuting this war.

So if our legislation passes--we will have to get the permission of our friends in Europe, but we have talked with many of them, and I think they will agree--we will give Ukraine an influx of $300 billion-- no taxpayer money from an American will be spent on this.
We are going to see what Mr. Putin is made of.
I don't want Putin to be the world's policeman either.
I don't want the Ayatollah in Iran to be the world's policeman.
Xi in China, Putin in Russia, and the Ayatollah in Iran are working together.
Putin couldn't prosecute this war without China.
Putin and Xi and the Ayatollah are working together.
The quarterback, in my opinion, is Xi; it is not Putin.
And here is their goal: Their goal is to have Putin dominate Central and Eastern Europe, to have the Ayatollah dominate the Middle East, and Iran control the Middle East.
Israel has caused them to put that part of their plan on the back burner.
This fight in Ukraine is not just about Ukraine.

I can promise you, with $300 billion of new capital--none of which will be American taxpayer money--Ukraine can buy some missiles and get Mr. Putin's attention, and he will be inviting us to a summit, and he will be paying for lunch.

But as you know, President Trump has also said--and I certainly see his point of view--if I am going to do it on behalf of America, by God, Europe's got to do it because they are the ones most at risk.
Well here is what I think we ought to do--and I am introducing legislation to do this.
And we are going to move this legislation.
If our legislation passes, here is what we will do.
We will seize that $300 billion--no longer freeze it; we will seize it.
We are going to level the playing field.
We are going to make it very, very costly--if we do this--for him to prosecute that war.
And I am going to tell you, that is not a world that is safe for freedom.

And the JCPOA just said to Iran: If you will stop moving toward a nuclear weapon, we--meaning the United States of America and the other countries that are part of the United Nations--will remove the sanctions that we had placed on Iran for trying to develop a nuclear weapon.
So Iran said: Pinky promise, we will stop building a nuclear weapon.
And, of course, the Ayatollah and Iran continued to develop a weapon.
Just because we have destroyed--``we'' meaning the United States of America--many of Iran's facilities to make that weapon does not mean that the issue has been resolved.
Iran has refused to come to the table, even still, to negotiate a settlement, a new JCPOA.

Of course, my preference would be to have Iran come to the table again before then and sit down with the United States and other members of the United Nations and resolve this issue of them having a nuclear weapon, but I don't expect that to happen.
The sanctions, which will be on Iranian banking, on Iranian shipping, oil, and arms are only part of the story.
But just because the sanctions have been brought back on Iran, that doesn't mean that they will be enforced.
I don't want to see this get lost in our discussion about the importance of the Ukraine situation and other issues of national security.
And unfortunately--I wish we didn't have to do it because I feel for the Iranian people.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Executive Calendar)
statements.title: One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Executive Calendar)
sentences: Some of my friends and colleagues talk about, well, all you did was stop the tax increase on billionaires.
Half of that tax increase would have hit working men and working women and working families in this country.
We made some of those tax cuts permanent.
We cut taxes on Social Security.
We expanded a tax credit for childcare to help moms and dads pay for the childcare so they can work.
For years and years and years, I have tried--we all have tried, many of us have tried--to provide the American people--moms and dads--with school choice.
We are doing that with the school choice portion of this bill.
We increase money for the border, and we increase money for defense.
We also address the problem in Medicaid.
And I have been very disappointed because some commentators have said that we are going to throw off from the Medicaid rolls, I have read, anywhere from 10 to 12 million people.
The implication in some of these articles and some of these comments is that we are just going to look at the Medicaid rolls and go through and say: You are gone.
The first thing you have to realize is that, actually, Medicaid is not going to be cut at all under this bill.
Under our bill that we just passed, our spending on Medicaid over the next 10 years is going to go up 20 percent, so nobody is cutting Medicaid.
There are some people, as a result of the new provisions that we have put into law, who will no longer be eligible for Medicaid and will no longer get Medicaid.
So when you say: Well, you are throwing people off of Medicaid-- they weren't entitled to it in the first place.
You are not entitled to Medicaid if you are making $200,000 a year and you didn't tell the truth when you signed up for Medicaid in your State and your State didn't verify your status.
Our bill is going to change the law so that 2.8 million Americans--the CBO says, like, we are throwing 10 or 12 million Americans off of Medicaid.
I will just give you this one example: 2.8 million of those Americans who will lose Medicaid are doubledippers.
We have 1.2 million people on the Medicaid rolls who are signed up in two States, and the American taxpayer is paying twice.
As you know, Mr. President, well--you were a great Governor; you were a Governor and a damn good one--most States use managed care, and they pay per Medicaid person.

So if a State is paying, let's say--I will pick a number--$8,000 per Medicaid patient per year to the healthcare organization to provide their care, and that person is signed up in two States, they are doubledipping, and it is costing the American taxpayer two $8,000 payments a year.
So from one perspective, you are throwing these people off of Medicaid--they weren't entitled to doubledip in the first place.
By ``CMS,'' I mean the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which is the Federal Agency that administers Medicare and Medicaid.
CMS has also found that there are 1.6 million people who are on Medicaid today who are receiving both Medicaid and ObamaCare.
Medicaid is supposed to be for the poor and disabled, and Medicare is for the elderly, and a lot of other Americans have health insurance through their job.

But there are a certain number of Americans who don't have health insurance because they are not old enough for Medicare, they are not poor enough for Medicaid, and maybe their employer doesn't offer health insurance.
So they can go to an exchange--we call them the ObamaCare exchange--and buy health insurance.

Now, President Obama and some of my colleagues--I wasn't here then, but when we passed the ObamaCare, the ObamaCare exchanges, the Affordable Care Act, we were told that health insurance would be cheaper, and we were told it would be more accessible.

But the point is that we have a number of Americans who, if they don't qualify for Medicare, they don't qualify for Medicaid, they don't get insurance through their employer, they go to the ObamaCare exchanges.
CMS found we have got 1.6 million people who are getting both health insurance through the ObamaCare exchanges--which we subsidize, taxpayers do--and through Medicaid.
CBO can put out all the reports that they want to saying: Oh, you are throwing all these people off Medicaid.
And technically, they are right, but they are not eligible to be on Medicaid.
Is that throwing people off of Medicaid?
But, once again, as the other provisions in this bill also do, we are taking people off Medicaid who weren't eligible for it in the first place.
That is $140 billion that we are going to save, and that savings is going to go back into Medicaid to make it even stronger.
I will just hit the highlights.
I will refresh everyone's memory.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: Rescissions (Executive Calendar)
statements.title: Rescissions (Executive Calendar)
sentences: Today, we are going to start talking about and voting on the rescission package, and I want to talk about that for a few minutes.
It is called a rescission bill or a rescission package.
President Trump has sent us a rescission bill, or a rescission package, asking the U.S. Congress to cut the budget by roughly $9 billion, and that is what we are going to start voting on today.
Since day one, the President, if you have paid attention to the news, has been working very hard to reduce government spending, and he has reduced a lot.
Mr. Musk, of course, has left, but the quest to reduce government spending--wasteful government spending, which I call spending porn--continues.
We have got a $37 trillion debt.
The only way to permanently reduce spending is to have Congress act, and that is what the President is asking us to do in this rescission bill.
The rescission package that the President has sent over--we are going to start considering it today.

After all of us on my side of the aisle have told the world that we need to reduce spending, if we vote against this rescission package and refuse to reduce spending by one-tenth of 1 percent of the budget, we ought to hide our heads in a bag.
That is important because not all government spending is wasteful, but a lot of it is.

The President, in light of our $37 trillion budget deficit, is asking us to reduce spending--to reduce a program--in the amount of $3.9 million for the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and intersex population in the Western Balkans.
The President is suggesting that we eliminate a program of $1 million for voter ID programs in Haiti.
The President is asking us to reduce the budget by $3 million which is appropriated for ``sexual reproductive health in Venezuela''; $3 million for circumcision, vasectomies, and condoms in Zambia.

There is $3 million for ``Sesame Street'' in Iraq; $833,000 for transgender people, sex workers, and their clients in Nepal; $882,000 for social media mentorship in Serbia and Belarus; $3.6 million for pastry cooking classes, cyber cafes, and dance focus groups for male prostitutes in Haiti.
We have $6.2 million for Venezuelan migrants in Colombia and $500,000 to buy Rwanda electric buses.
If they want electric buses, they have got a budget.
There is $300,000 for a pride parade in Lesotho; $300,000 for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex advocacy in Uganda; $500,000 for biodiversity in Peru.
Congress didn't vote to spend $3 million on sexual reproductive health in Venezuela; we voted for a program that the bureaucrats took and spent on sexual health, reproductive health, in Venezuela.
I am going to read you some of the appropriations that the President is asking us to eliminate from the current budget, and you be the judge.
Well, I am going to tell you why: We didn't.
He is asking us to cut a little over $1 billion for what I will call public broadcasting.

We are going to start public broadcasting, and we are going to give them money every year, and they won't have to run ads because we are going to spend taxpayer money to give to these radio stations and television stations.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: Russia (Executive Calendar)
statements.title: Russia (Executive Calendar)
sentences: I want to talk first about Russia and the war with Ukraine.
Now, regardless of how you feel about the war in Ukraine, I think most fairminded people can agree on two things.
No. 1, Vladimir Putin, who runs Russia--not the people of Russia but their leadership--is a thug.

President Trump has tried, and, frankly, President Putin has treated our President--as I have said before on the Senate floor, Putin has treated our President like President Trump has taken the bullet train to chump town.
I think he has disrespected America--``he'' meaning President Putin--and I think he has disrespected President Trump.

I think Ukraine is willing to negotiate a reasonable settlement, but it takes two to tango, and we are not going to have a settlement until President Putin decides it is in his best interest to stop the war, not in Russia's best interest because I don't think he cares about his people.

I think the war will stop when Putin thinks it is in his best interest, and I don't think he is going to think it is in his best interest until he feels the pressure because dealing with Putin is like dealing with most tyrants: It is like hand- feeding a shark.
A lot of people think of Russia and think of Putin as this gigantic country with a lot of wealth and power, and that is not really the case.
Putin relies on oil revenues for about a third of his budget.
Remember, I said Putin depends on oil for about 30 percent to a third of his revenue, and the price of oil is down.
No. 2, Russia is spending all of its money fighting the war with Ukraine, which has hurt other parts of its economy.

The point I am trying to make is, when you are dealing with a tyrant like Putin and you are trying to bring him to the negotiating table, what you have to do is get him down and choke him, and the way to get President Putin down and choke him is through his cashflow.
Putin--and, remember, I am not talking about the good people in Russia.
I am talking about Vladimir Putin, the thug.
Putin is only able to prosecute his war through cashflow generated by his sale of oil.
For example, India is buying a lot of Russia's oil.

It would say to those who want to buy Russian oil: If you want to buy Russian oil, have at it--knock yourself out--but you are not going to be able to do business with America, and you are not going to be able to use the American dollar, which is the world's currency, to do business in America.
It will put Putin on his knees within 3 months, and he won't have any choice but to come to the bargaining table.
I remember when President Biden said to Putin: Well, you know, we don't want you to go into Ukraine, but if it is just a little excursion, it might be OK.
President Trump, on the other hand, has really tried to be rational and negotiate with Putin and say: Look, we need to have an amicable solution to satisfy both sides.
Putin has done nothing but embarrass our President and our country.
I hate to see it for the Russian people, but the time has come to put Putin on his knees, to get him down and choke him.

The President is the one who is trying to negotiate the peace, but I hope President Trump will seriously consider letting us pull the trigger because it is the only thing--it is the only thing-- that is going to get Vladimir Putin to the table.
And some of them run countries, and one of them is Vladimir Putin.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: Russia (Executive Calendar)
statements.title: Russia (Executive Calendar)
sentences: I ask that question in light of what has been happening over the past week in Iran.
You couldn't find either one of them with a search party. ``Dog the Bounty Hunter,'' all of a sudden, couldn't find President Putin.
I thought Iran and Russia were peeps.
I mean, for decades, Iran and Russia have had a partnership where they have attacked everyone in the freedom-loving West.
Now, I know Iran has a relationship with China, but that is more transactional.
China just likes to buy Iran's cheap oil.
With Russia and Iran, it was supposed to be a deeper, more meaningful relationship.
I remember when Putin invaded Ukraine.
One of the first allies he turned to was Iran, and Iran sent Russia ammunition, and Iran sent Russia artillery shells, and Iran sent Russia drones.
Iran has sent Russia drones and ammunition and artillery shells every single day of the war.
I mean, it hasn't been a good week for Iran.
On Monday of this week, Iran's top diplomat met with President Putin and asked for help.
Do you know what President Putin said he would provide?
You know, it is not the first time that we have seen President Putin's true colors.
You would think that Iran would learn.
The month after Iran, through Hamas, attacked Israel back in October of 2023, Iran immediately asked Moscow to supply Iran with-- because Iran knew what was coming, and so did Hamas.
They knew retribution was coming from Israel.
Iran asked Moscow for jet fighters, for attack helicopters, air defense systems, and training jets, and Iran was sure that their buddy Putin would be there.
Putin sent them a few jets and said: Go away.
Then, not long ago, when Israel took out the better part of Iran's air defense system, its golden dome--it wasn't exactly golden.
Iran asked Russia, said: Look, we have to rearm.
We need more air defense missiles to shoot down the Israeli planes.
President Putin said: Go away.
President Putin has done it to other countries.
Russia has had alliances not just with Iran through the years.
Iran and Russia worked together to prop up al-Assad in Syria.
Iran, yes, but especially Russia.
He went to Mr. Putin and said: Help me.
Mr. Putin said: No. You are on your own.
I will give you a couple of examples.

statements.where: Floor speech, Congressional Record: Education (Executive Calendar)
statements.title: Education (Executive Calendar)
sentences: They have implemented successfully school-choice programs.
They can send their child to a charter school.
Charter schools are tuition-free.
Charter schools are public schools.

sentences: The first topic I would like to talk about--I know it is very sensitive--is trade and tariffs.
There are really only two reasons why a country would impose a tariff, and every country in the world, to my knowledge, does have tariffs.
There are only two reasons for a country to impose a tariff: first, for national security.

So if China is determined to--let me try to use a more neutral word-- to undermine the United States of America, I could see where we would limit, want to limit, some of our goods such as, let's say, semiconductor design equipment.
That is what I mean by ``national security.'' But the other reason, and the reason that most countries use the tariff, is to protect the domestic industry.
We want to protect our king cake bakers here in Alabama, so we are going to impose a tariff.
Let's suppose they impose a $4 tariff.
Now, my personal opinion is that most Alabamians, who are very smart people, would pay extra for the Louisiana king cake because it is so much better, but that is how tariffs work.

If you have a domestic industry, like a king cake bakery, and you want to protect it from competition to allow it to grow and employ the people in that particular country, maybe you impose a tax, a tariff, on folks on the outside of your country who want to sell into your country.

President Trump, who believes passionately in the virtue of tariffs, thinks that the tariffs ought to be equal.

I am not suggesting that I agree with the President on everything about tariffs, but when you have got your neighboring country and good friend that is 8 times smaller than you are, and in terms of population, it is 10 times smaller than you are, and your neighbor is selling $63 billion more in goods to you than you are selling to them, that seems kind of unfair.
